abstract: Cortical extratelencephalic neurons (ET) derive from either direct neurogenesis from radial glia cells (ETd) or indirect neurogenesis through intermediate progenitors (ETi), but whether and how neurogenic origin contributes to ET diversity and function remains unknown. Using genetic strategies that differentially target ETd and ETi, we profiled their transcriptomes across the isocortex and imaged their activity in motor cortex during a reach-grasp-drink (RGD) task. While both ETd and ETi contribute to all transcriptomically-defined ET subtypes, they diverge significantly in the concerted expression profile of effector-gene families that shape transcriptional regulation, neuronal connectivity and physiology. During the RGD task, motor cortex ETd formed a small yet heterogeneous pool of broadly tuned activity archetypes, while ETi included a diversified set of spatially organized subpopulations that tracked successive actions of RGD. Therefore, neurogenic origin defines a developmental axis of neuronal diversification orthogonal to the current transcriptomic classification scheme, in which ETi differ from ETd transcriptomically through coordinated significant shifts in effector-gene families, while functionally in the motor cortex, they elaborate a small pool of task-generic ETd into specialized output channels that track different phases of goal-directed RGD behavior.
